group.line: A partitioned log keeps each document's events in order, compare-and-set drops stale ones, durable workflows retry and resume, and tombstones, backfill, cursors and a dead-letter queue keep it honest.
group.dumb: Every change becomes a small note on a conveyor belt. Notes about the same document stay in order, and old or repeated notes are thrown away. A careful worker handles each note, and if it fails it tries again a few times, then parks the note where a person can look. Deletes are handled first and fastest, and the bookmark only moves when the work is safely saved.

ch_bus.line:
Partitioned append-only log keyed by (tenant, doc), at-least-once delivery
partition = hash(tenant_id, doc_id) mod P ; commit offset after apply
ch_bus.dumb: All change notes go onto one long belt that is split into lanes. A note's lane is picked from its tenant and document, so two notes about the same document always share a lane and stay in order. A worker marks a note as done only after handling it, so a crash means it sees the note again, never that it loses it.
ch_bus.inn: Events from ch_hook, ch_delta, ch_cdc, ch_sweep, ch_fill and so_norm: envelope {uri, app, tenant, kind, version, content_hash, modified_at, acl_ref} plus {lane 'live' or 'backfill'}.
ch_bus.out: Ordered events per partition to ch_dedupe and to ll_sub subscribers; consumer offsets per group.
ch_bus.store: The log itself: envelopes only, never document bodies, retained 7 days (default, design) so a bug fix can replay. Offsets stored per consumer group.
ch_bus.fail: A producer write that is not acknowledged is retried 3 times over 2 s, then the producer returns an error to its caller (the receiver then answers 503). A lost partition replica is replaced from the other 2 of 3 copies (design); a consumer that crashes restarts at its last committed offset.
ch_bus.req: Requirement: 'through APIs, webhooks and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers'
ch_bus.hard: The log engine (Kafka, Redpanda or a database-backed queue) is not chosen; the choice depends on the volume at the first tenant.
ch_bus.prop: Proposal: one ordered buffer between fast producers and rate-limited workers lets each side run at its own pace and makes replay possible.

deep.purpose: Decouple producers from consumers, keep events for one document in order, and make every event replayable for 7 days.
expected: Events for one (tenant, doc) always land in the same partition in arrival order
Backfill traffic never delays live events because they use separate lanes (t_t45)
A consumer can rewind to any offset inside the retention window
not_expected: It does not drop duplicates; at-least-once means duplicates are normal and ch_dedupe removes them
It does not hold document bodies or secrets
It does not give global ordering, only per-document ordering

algorithm.name: Partitioned append-only log with keyed ordering
algorithm.formula: partition = hash(tenant_id || doc_id) mod P ; delivery = at-least-once ; order = per partition
steps: Compute the partition from the tenant and document id so the key never splits
Append the envelope and wait for acknowledgement from 2 of 3 replicas (design)
Consumers read in offset order and commit the offset only after ch_dedupe finishes
Keep live and backfill as separate topics with separate consumer groups and separate rate shares
Expire segments after 7 days

params.P: 64 partitions per lane (default; tune to peak events per second)
params.retention: 7 days (design; long enough for a weekend outage)
params.per_connector_queue: one queue and token bucket per (tenant, connector), t_t48

definitions: s: skew factor of the busiest key group, at least 1
m: events one consumer applies per second
math.formula_full: load_per_partition = s * r / P ; consumers_needed = ceil(s * r / (P * m)) * P
math.derivation: Hashing spreads keys evenly, so the average partition sees r / P events per second. Hot tenants raise the busiest partition by a skew factor.
math.worked_example: r = 5,000 events/s, P = 64, s = 3: busiest partition 3 * 5,000 / 64 = 234 events/s. If one consumer applies m = 100 events/s, that partition needs 3 consumers in a group, but a partition allows one consumer, so P is raised to 192 or the apply path is sped up.
math.complexity: O(1) append and O(1) read per event; partition lookup is a hash.
failure_modes: Hot key (one doc edited constantly): same partition by design; ch_dedupe collapses repeats and coalescing in the producer limits it
Too few partitions cap parallelism: raise P with a new generation of the topic and drain the old one
math.calibration: Pick P so the busiest partition runs under 60% of one consumer at the 7-day peak; review monthly.

alternatives.name: Per-document queues
alternatives.why_rejected: Millions of queues; ordering by hash on a partitioned log gets the same guarantee.

alternatives.name: Direct call from producer to worker
alternatives.why_rejected: No buffer when an app rate-limits us; a backlog would block the receiver.

security: Cross-tenant read: a consumer must not see another tenant's events; tenant id is in every key and topic ACLs and consumer credentials are per lane, with row policy as a second check at ch_dedupe
Forged event injection by a compromised producer: producers hold write-only credentials per connector and the envelope carries the connector id, checked at read
Sensitive data in the log: envelopes hold ids, versions and hashes only; bodies never enter, so the 7-day retention holds no content
Poison event crashing consumers in a loop: bounded retries downstream then parked in ch_dlq

performance.slo: p95 under 100 ms from append to first consumer read; 5,000 events/s sustained (design target)
performance.scaling: At 10x (50,000 events/s) the partition count and consumer groups scale out; the first limit is the number of partitions, solved by a new topic generation.

edge_cases: Empty lane: consumers idle, no error
Duplicate events: expected, removed by ch_dedupe
Huge envelope above 64 KB: rejected at append; only ids belong in it
Concurrent producers for the same document: both land in one partition in append order
Partition leader loss: failover to a replica, producers retry within the 2 s budget
Clock skew: ordering is by offset, never by timestamp
New app joins: it needs only a producer credential and a lane key, and its envelope comes from the connector manifest (so_sdk) or the MCP bridge (so_mcp) through so_norm

tests.name: per-document order
tests.given: three versions (1, 2, 3) of one doc appended by two producers
tests.expect: read in append order from one partition

tests.name: crash replay
tests.given: consumer applies offset 100 and dies before commit
tests.expect: restart reads offset 100 again, ch_dedupe drops the duplicate

tests.name: lane isolation
tests.given: backfill lane holds 1,000,000 events, live lane gets 1
tests.expect: the live event is read within 100 ms

tests.name: retention
tests.expect: gone; consumer asking for it is told to resync via ch_sweep

cost_levers: 7-day retention and ids-only envelopes keep storage tiny
Coalesce repeated events for one document before append
feedback_events: Consumer lag and replays per consumer group feed partition-count and retention tuning

repos.name: Debezium
repos.take: Ships changes into Kafka-style logs, the transport model we use

deep.industry: Notion uses Kafka consumers for live edits and a separate batch path for onboarding (t_t45); per-connector queues are a common pattern because limits differ (t_t48).

ch_dedupe.line:
Compare-and-set on (doc_id, source_version): apply only if newer than stored
UPDATE ... WHERE doc_id = :d AND version < :v
ch_dedupe.dumb: Because notes can arrive twice or out of order, we check each one against what we already know about the document. If the note is about a version we already have, or an older one, we throw it away. If it is newer, we let it through. This makes it safe to repeat any note any number of times.
ch_dedupe.inn: Ordered event per document key from ch_bus {uri, tenant, kind, version, content_hash, modified_at}; stored {version, content_hash, deleted_at} for the document from ix_ptr; tombstone floor version from ch_tomb.
ch_dedupe.out: Events that beat the stored version to ch_wf; events that fail validation or repeat failures to ch_dlq; a drop counter per reason.
ch_dedupe.store: Reads ix_ptr row version and tombstone floor. Writes only the idempotency record {tenant, doc_id, version} with a 7-day TTL (design); the version itself is written later by ch_wf with the same compare-and-set.
ch_dedupe.fail: If ix_ptr is unavailable the event is retried 5 times with backoff 200 ms to 3 s, then parked in ch_dlq with class 'store_unavailable'. A lost compare-and-set race (another worker wrote first) is re-read once and decided again.
ch_dedupe.req: Requirement: 'Ingest documents and messages; answer with citations; respect source permissions'
ch_dedupe.hard: Some apps give etags that are not ordered; the tie-break uses modified_at then content hash, and per-app version semantics need a table.
ch_dedupe.prop: Proposal: delta replays and duplicate pushes are normal (t_t55, t_t05), so apply must be safe to repeat and safe to reorder.

deep.purpose: Make processing idempotent and order-safe, so duplicates, replays and out-of-order arrivals never overwrite newer state.
expected: The same event applied twice changes state once
An older version arriving after a newer one is dropped
A delete event with a version at least the stored one wins, and an older event cannot resurrect the document
not_expected: It does not fetch content or compute hashes of bodies
It does not retry failed work; ch_wf does
It does not need a lock across documents

algorithm.name: Version compare-and-set
algorithm.formula: apply(e) iff e.version > stored.version (or e.modified_at > stored.modified_at when versions are not ordered) and e.version > tombstone_floor
steps: Read stored version and tombstone floor for (tenant, doc_id)
If the app's versions are ordered numbers, compare them; if they are etags, compare modified_at and then content_hash inequality
If the event is not newer, drop it and count the reason (duplicate or stale)
If newer, pass it to ch_wf; the final write repeats the compare-and-set so a race cannot lose
Record the idempotency key so a replay in the next 7 days is dropped in O(1)

definitions: d: duplicate rate of the source
math.formula_full: apply iff v_e > max(v_s, f); work_saved = d / (1 + d) of events dropped
math.derivation: A strictly greater version means the event has information the store lacks. Equal means seen, lower means stale. Duplicates are therefore dropped at one indexed read each.
math.worked_example: Stored v = 7. Arrivals in order: v8, v8, v6, v9. v8 applies (8 > 7); second v8 drops (8 > 8 is false); v6 drops; v9 applies. Two of four events reach ch_wf. If a delete with version 9 sets floor 9, a late v8 is dropped because 8 > 9 is false.
math.complexity: O(1) indexed lookup per event, no scans.
failure_modes: Source versions reset (app restore from backup): versions go backward; the event is held in ch_dlq class 'version_regression' for an operator, who can accept a reset epoch
Etag with no order and equal modified_at: compare content_hash, apply on difference to be safe, since a repeat apply is idempotent
math.calibration: Watch the drop ratio per app; a stale-drop rate above 5% for an app with ordered versions points to a producer fault.

alternatives.name: Distributed lock per document
alternatives.why_rejected: Adds a lock service and a failure mode; compare-and-set needs only the row.

alternatives.name: Exactly-once delivery
alternatives.why_rejected: Not achievable end to end across an external app; at-least-once plus idempotent apply gives the same result.

security: Replay of an old event to roll back a document: the tombstone floor and version compare drop it
Version inflation by a malicious app user setting a huge version to block later real changes: versions are bounded to the stored plus a sanity ceiling (design) and the sweep re-lists real versions
Cross-tenant version collision: the key is (tenant, doc_id), never doc_id alone
Idempotency table growth as a denial of service: TTL of 7 days and a per-tenant cap

performance.slo: p95 under 5 ms per event (design); 5,000 events/s per cluster
performance.scaling: At 10x (50,000 events/s) the ix_ptr read path is the limit; the idempotency check runs first from a cache and partitions by tenant.

edge_cases: Missing stored row: treated as version 0, first event applies
Duplicate within the same second: idempotency key drops it
Event with null version: modified_at used; if both null, held in ch_dlq class 'no_version'
Delete then create with the same id: create needs a version above the floor
Concurrent events for one doc on two workers: the partition guarantees one reader, the final compare-and-set guards anyway
Clock skew: not used when versions are ordered; modified_at compares only the app's own timestamps
Unicode ids: compared as bytes after NFC normalisation by so_norm

tests.name: race
tests.given: two workers both read v7 and write v8 and v9

cost_levers: Dropping duplicates early saves a fetch and an embedding per repeat
Content hash equality skips re-derivation when only metadata moved
feedback_events: Drop reasons per app expose producers that replay too often
deep.industry: Microsoft and GitHub both document replays and redelivery, so idempotent apply keyed by id and version is the standard answer (t_t55, t_t05).

ch_wf.line:
Durable workflow: bounded retries, resumable cursor, per-source concurrency cap
delay = min(300 s, 2 s * 2^n) with jitter; max 6 attempts
ch_wf.dumb: This is the worker that actually processes each change. It saves its progress after every step, so if the machine dies it carries on from the last step instead of starting over. If an app is slow or says 'too many requests', it waits and tries again a few times with longer pauses. After the last try it parks the note for a person.
ch_wf.inn: Events that beat the stored version from ch_dedupe; operator replays from ch_dlq; pause and stop orders from op_health and gv_kill; rate budgets from so_rate.
ch_wf.out: Pointer upsert to ix_ptr, derive request {uri, version} to ix_fetch, delete events to ch_tomb, ACL refresh orders to ac_src, cursor commit to ch_cursor, exhausted events to ch_dlq.
ch_wf.store: Workflow history in the durable engine (ids, versions and step results only, no bodies or tokens); cursor and watermark in ch_cursor. Workflow id is (tenant, app, stream) so a stream has one owner.
ch_wf.fail: Each step retries up to 6 attempts with delays of about 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 s (62 s total before jitter), honouring Retry-After when the app sends it (t_t06, t_t08). After 6 failed attempts the event goes to ch_dlq with the error class and history. A worker crash resumes from the last completed step with no repeat of finished steps.
ch_wf.hard: Temporal is a style reference; the engine choice, the cluster run cost and the history size limit are open.
ch_wf.prop: Proposal: long syncs fail midway all the time; resuming from a checkpoint beats restarting (t_t10).

deep.purpose: Run each change through upsert, derive and permission refresh as a resumable, rate-limited, bounded-retry workflow so nothing is lost or repeated.
expected: A crash resumes at the last completed step with no duplicate side effects
Concurrent work per source never exceeds its rate budget
An event that keeps failing ends in ch_dlq after the retry bound, not in an endless loop
not_expected: It does not decide freshness; ch_dedupe already filtered stale events
It does not store document bodies in history
It does not retry forever

algorithm.name: Durable execution with exponential backoff, jitter and cursor checkpoints
algorithm.formula: delay_n = min(cap, base * 2^n) * U(0.5, 1.0) ;  attempts <= 6 ;  concurrency <= budget share
steps: Take a slot from the per-(tenant, app) concurrency limit set by so_rate
Run the steps in order: upsert pointer, request derive, refresh access list, each an idempotent activity keyed by (doc_id, version)
On a retryable error wait the backoff or the app's Retry-After, whichever is longer
After the last step commit cursor and watermark with the events (ch_cursor)
After 6 attempts send the event and its history to ch_dlq

params.concurrency: per (tenant, app) from the rate budget, t_t48

math.formula_full: S = sum_{n=0}^{4} min(cap, base*2^n) = base*(2^5 - 1) when cap not reached
math.derivation: Doubling waits give a slow app time to recover while the total wait stays bounded. Jitter spreads retries so many workflows do not hit the app at the same instant.
math.worked_example: base 2 s, 6 attempts, 5 waits: 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 = 62 s before jitter; with U between 0.5 and 1.0 the total is between 31 s and 62 s. A Jira 429 with Retry-After 90 s overrides the 2 s step and waits 90 s.
math.complexity: O(steps) per event; history grows O(events) per run, reset by continue-as-new.
failure_modes: Retry storm after an app outage: jitter plus the concurrency cap stop it
Hourly quota exhausted: Jira blocks until the next UTC hour (t_t06), so the workflow sleeps to that time instead of retrying
math.calibration: If more than 1% of events reach the DLQ with transient errors, raise attempts to 8 and the cap to 600 s.

alternatives.name: Plain queue worker with retry count
alternatives.why_rejected: Loses position on a crash and cannot resume a long multi-step job (t_t10).

alternatives.name: Cron script per connector
alternatives.why_rejected: No history, no resumption, no per-source concurrency control.

security: Secret in workflow history: history is durable and readable by operators; activities fetch tokens from so_oauth by reference and history holds ids only
Confused deputy: a workflow for tenant A must never use tenant B's token; the workflow id and the token reference carry the tenant and the activity checks it
Poison event retrying forever to exhaust budget: attempts bounded at 6 and then parked
Operator replay abuse: replay needs an operator role and writes an audit record

performance.slo: p95 under 2 s per event from apply to pointer upsert when the app is healthy (design)
performance.scaling: At 10x event rate the durable engine's history writes limit; shard by tenant namespace and keep history small by storing ids only.

edge_cases: App outage of 2 h: retries stop at 6 attempts and events go to ch_dlq; replay after recovery
Worker killed mid-step: resumes at that step; the step is idempotent
Duplicate event reaching it: the final compare-and-set makes it a no-op
Huge event burst for one stream: concurrency cap queues the rest
Partial failure (pointer written, derive failed): derive retries alone; pointer stays at the new version, flagged unverified until derived
Clock skew: uses engine time for timers, never the app's clock
Pause order from op_health: finishes the current step and holds the rest

tests.name: resume after crash
tests.given: worker killed after the pointer upsert step
tests.expect: restart runs derive next and does not repeat the upsert

tests.name: bounded retries
tests.expect: 6 attempts over about 62 s then one event in ch_dlq with the history

tests.name: concurrency cap
tests.expect: never more than 5 app calls in flight

cost_levers: Skip derive when content_hash is unchanged
Per-source caps avoid paying for throttled calls
feedback_events: DLQ rate and retry counts per app tune max_attempts and caps

repos.name: Temporal
repos.take: Durable execution with retries and long-running state; the style we adopt

deep.industry: Anthropic built resume-from-checkpoint after restarting from scratch proved too costly (t_t10).

ch_fill.line:
Priority crawl: recent, shared and popular first; paced to half the quota
score = 0.5 * recency + 0.3 * shared + 0.2 * popular
ch_fill.dumb: When an app is first connected there may be millions of items. We do not crawl in a random order. We start with the newest, most shared and most viewed items, so search is useful within minutes. We also use only half of the app's request allowance, so live changes are never held up by the big first crawl.
ch_fill.inn: Connect event and capability descriptor for a new app, request share from ch_sched, listing pages with {object_id, modified_at, shared_count, view_count}.
ch_fill.out: Backfill batch {uri, rank} on the backfill lane of ch_bus; progress watermark to ch_cursor.
ch_fill.store: Reads app listings. Writes a crawl frontier {stream, next_page_token, ranked queue head} and the watermark through ch_cursor; no document text.
ch_fill.fail: On a 429 it waits Retry-After and halves its pace for 10 min. If a page fails 3 times it skips it and records the gap for op_cov, then continues. A crash resumes from the saved frontier; after 24 h with no progress it pages op_health.
ch_fill.req: Requirement: 'through APIs, webhooks and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers'
ch_fill.hard: Slack and similar live-only sources get pointers via live search, not a crawl (t_t07, t_t13); the popularity signal is missing in many apps and falls back to recency.
ch_fill.prop: Proposal: a first crawl can take hours (t_t08); ordering by value makes search useful before it ends, on a lane that cannot slow live sync (t_t45).

deep.purpose: Make search useful early by crawling the most valuable items first, at a pace that leaves the live path untouched.
expected: The top 10% by score is indexed before the rest
Live events keep their freshness while a backfill runs
Progress is visible as a coverage percentage and resumable after a stop
not_expected: It does not copy document text; it lists and sends pointers to the bus
It does not exceed its share of the rate budget
It does not backfill live-only sources such as Slack text

algorithm.name: Priority-ordered frontier with paced crawl
algorithm.formula: score = w_r * exp(-age_days / 30) + w_s * min(1, ln(1 + shared) / ln(101)) + w_p * min(1, ln(1 + views) / ln(101)) ; rate <= 0.5 * quota
steps: List the app's top-level containers and fetch their metadata page by page
Score each item and push to a priority queue; crawl in descending score
Send ranked batches to the backfill lane of ch_bus
Pace requests so use stays at or under half the hourly quota (t_t06 estimate)
Write the progress watermark with each batch so a restart resumes

params.w_r_w_s_w_p: 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 (default; tune against which items users ask about first)

definitions: w_r, w_s, w_p: weights summing to 1
c: cost per object in quota points
math.formula_full: objects_per_hour = 0.5 * Q / c ; crawl_hours = N / objects_per_hour
math.derivation: Recency decays exponentially, sharing and popularity grow slowly with a log so one huge number cannot dominate. Pacing at half the quota leaves the other half for live traffic and sweeps.
math.worked_example: Doc A: 2 days old, shared with 40, 10 views: recency = exp(-2/30) = 0.935; shared = ln41/ln101 = 0.805; popular = ln11/ln101 = 0.520; score = 0.5*0.935 + 0.3*0.805 + 0.2*0.520 = 0.813. Doc B: 400 days old, private (1 person), no views: 0.5*0 + 0.3*0.150 + 0 = 0.045. A crawls first. Pace: a Jira tenant with 200 users has about 100,000 + 10*200 = 102,000 points/h (t_t06); half is 51,000; at an assumed 2 points per object (the identity-read price in t_t06) that is 25,500 objects/h, so 500,000 objects take 19.6 h.
math.complexity: O(N log N) for the priority queue over N items, O(N / page) requests.
failure_modes: Weights favour recency so old but important policy documents wait: expose a manual pin list
Popularity unavailable: weight set to 0 and the remainder renormalised
math.calibration: After 2 weeks, compare the crawl rank of items users actually retrieved; move weights so 80% of retrieved items sit in the top 20% by score.

alternatives.name: Crawl in listing order
alternatives.why_rejected: Hours before anything useful is searchable.

alternatives.name: Full speed crawl
alternatives.why_rejected: Exhausts hourly quotas and starves live sync (t_t09).

security: Backfill reading more than the connector should: it uses the same scoped token as live sync and skips containers the admin excluded
Quota starvation of a customer's own users by the crawl: hard 50% share and 10 min backoff after any 429
Poisoned metadata (huge shared counts to jump the queue): counts are capped by the log scale and the first crawl visits everything eventually
Cross-tenant frontier mix-up: frontier state keyed by (tenant, app, stream)

performance.slo: top 10% indexed within 1 h of connect for an app of 100,000 objects (design)
performance.complexity: O(N log N) ordering, N / page requests
performance.scaling: At 10x objects the quota, not our compute, is the limit (t_t08); the crawl takes longer, and coverage is shown to the admin.

edge_cases: Empty app: finishes at once with coverage 100%
Huge item (a 2 GB file): pointer only, body fetched later on demand
Duplicate listing of the same object across pages: ch_dedupe drops it
Object changed during the crawl: live event arrives first and wins by version
Partial failure: skipped pages recorded as gaps for op_cov
Unicode names: ids used for ordering ties, never names
Item with no timestamps: ranked at the bottom

tests.name: priority order
tests.given: Doc A score 0.813 and Doc B 0.045

tests.name: quota share
tests.expect: no more than 51,000 points used in the hour

tests.name: live not delayed
tests.given: backfill running at full pace and a live event arrives
tests.expect: live event applied within the live SLO

cost_levers: Defer low-score items by days if the quota is tight
feedback_events: Which items users retrieve first retunes the score weights

repos.name: Airbyte
repos.take: Initial full sync then incremental is its default model; we add priority order

deep.industry: Notion runs an offline batch path for onboarding apart from the live path (t_t45); Notion's own API limits make big backfills slow by design (t_t08).

ch_tomb.line:
Delete or access removal soft-deletes the pointer now, purges derived data later
seconds to hide, 24 h to purge
ch_tomb.dumb: When a document is deleted, or a person loses access, we hide it from search straight away. We cannot trust that old search entries disappear on their own, so we also queue a cleanup that removes everything made from that document. We keep a small marker for a while so a late, old message cannot bring the document back.
ch_tomb.inn: Delete or access-removed event {uri, reason} from ch_wf (Graph '@removed' with reason, Drive removed items, t_t02, t_t04).
ch_tomb.out: Soft-delete flag on ix_ptr, purge order to ix_gc, tombstone {uri, tenant, reason, at} to gv_erase, floor version to ch_dedupe.
ch_tomb.store: Writes the tombstone row {tenant, uri, reason, at, floor_version} for 30 days (design) and the purge job status. Reads nothing else.
ch_tomb.fail: If the soft delete fails it retries 5 times over 10 s, and the document is hidden by the search filter on the next ACL cache refresh at the latest; a purge that fails retries hourly for 24 h and then pages an operator. Soft delete always runs before purge.
ch_tomb.req: Requirement: 'Ingest documents and messages; answer with citations; respect source permissions'
ch_tomb.hard: Soft-deleted vectors can persist in raw index files (t_t17, low confidence); hard delete must be proven by a probe test after compaction.
ch_tomb.prop: Proposal: stale hits on deleted or newly forbidden documents are the worst failure of an index, so hide first and clean after.

deep.purpose: Remove a deleted or no-longer-accessible document from search at once and from every derived store within a bound.
expected: The document stops appearing in search within seconds of the event being applied
Vectors, postings, snippets and access rows are purged within 24 h and verified
A late stale event cannot resurrect the document
not_expected: It does not delete anything in the source app
It does not remove the pointer row itself on the first step, only marks it
It does not handle a person's permission change without a delete; that goes through ac_src and ac_store

algorithm.name: Two-phase delete: soft delete now, queued purge, tombstone floor
algorithm.formula: hidden_at = event_applied_at + t_soft ; purged_at <= hidden_at + 24 h ; floor = event.version
steps: Set deleted_at and the reason on the ix_ptr row; the search pre-filter excludes it from then on
Write the tombstone with the floor version and send it to ch_dedupe
Queue purge of vectors, postings, snippets and ACL rows through ix_gc and gv_erase
After purge, run a probe query for the document's text and check zero hits using a strong read (t_t57)
Keep the tombstone 30 days to block resurrection, then drop it

params.purge_deadline: 24 h (design; tune to the tenant's legal terms)

definitions: t_lag: delivery lag of the change path
math.formula_full: exposure_window = t_lag + t_soft ; erasure_total = t_lag + t_soft + t_purge
math.derivation: A deleted document stays findable only while the change has not arrived and been applied. After that it is hidden, and later erased inside the purge window.
math.worked_example: Worst case on a Graph driveItem webhook path: t_lag 6 h (t_t01), t_soft 5 s, t_purge 24 h: hidden after 6 h 5 s, fully erased after 30 h 5 s. With a delta poll at 30 s the exposure window shrinks to about 35 s, which is why deletes also trigger an immediate live recheck at read time (ac_live).
math.complexity: O(chunks of the document) purge operations; one indexed write for the soft delete.
failure_modes: Soft-deleted vectors remain in index files (t_t17): compaction plus a probe test per purge
Tombstone dropped too early and a late event resurrects the document: retention 30 days exceeds the 7-day replay window
math.calibration: Test with 100 deletes per week: all must hit zero results by the probe; any miss shortens the purge deadline and adds compaction.

alternatives.name: Hard delete immediately
alternatives.why_rejected: Purge across several stores cannot be instant, and a failure midway leaves orphans with no record.

alternatives.name: Rely on the next sweep to find deletes
alternatives.why_rejected: The exposure window would be a week.

security: Zombie hit: a deleted or forbidden document still being returned; control is the soft-delete flag in the pre-filter plus the live recheck at read time
Resurrection by replayed event: the floor version in ch_dedupe blocks any event at or below it
Tombstone as a leak: it holds uri, reason and time only, not content or title
Erasure bypass through copies: derived embeddings are treated as personal data (t_t15, t_t16) and purged with the rest, and per-tenant keys allow crypto-shredding as a last resort (t_t17)

performance.slo: soft delete p95 under 5 s after the event is applied; purge complete within 24 h
performance.scaling: At 10x deletes (a mass delete of 1M items) the soft delete stays one write each; purge is batched and paced so it does not starve search.

edge_cases: Delete of an unknown document: tombstone still written so a late create below the floor is dropped
Trash then restore in the source: a newer version above the floor un-hides the pointer and re-derives
Bulk delete of 1M objects: soft delete first in batches of 10,000, purge paced
Permission removed but document alive: reason 'access_removed' hides it for that audience through the ACL path and keeps the pointer for others
Duplicate delete event: second is a no-op
Concurrent delete and update: higher version wins; equal version delete wins
Clock skew: floor uses source version, not time

deep.industry: Graph delta returns '@removed' with a reason and Drive returns removed items when asked (t_t02, t_t04); Microsoft lets admins disconnect and remove indexed content (t_t12).

ch_cursor.line:
Transactional {stream, cursor, watermark}, committed with the events it covers
fenced by epoch; lag = now - watermark
ch_cursor.dumb: This is the bookmark box. For each stream of changes it remembers how far we have read and how far everything is safely saved. The bookmark and the events it covers are written together, so they can never disagree. A counter on each bookmark stops an old, slow worker from overwriting a newer one.
ch_cursor.inn: Cursor commits from ch_wf {tenant, app, stream, cursor, watermark, epoch}; log positions from ch_cdc; backfill watermarks from ch_fill.
ch_cursor.out: Resume point {stream, cursor, epoch} to ch_delta; last full listing time to ch_sweep; watermark to op_lag.
ch_cursor.store: A relational table {tenant, app, stream, cursor, watermark, epoch, updated_at} and an outbox table of events, written in one transaction (outbox pattern, our design); cursors encrypted at rest.
ch_cursor.fail: A commit that loses the epoch check is rejected and the stale worker stops; the transaction retries 3 times over 1 s on a deadlock. If the table is down, pollers stop for up to 5 min and alert op_health, and nothing advances, so nothing is lost.
ch_cursor.req: Requirement: 'through APIs, webhooks and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers'
ch_cursor.hard: Whether the outbox relay is a polling loop or a log tail of the table is open; watermark rules for streams with many partitions need real traffic to tune.
ch_cursor.prop: Proposal: a cursor moved before its events are safe loses changes; committing both in one transaction is the only way to rule that out (t_t04).

deep.purpose: Guarantee that a saved position never gets ahead of the events it covers, and that only one worker owns a stream at a time.
expected: After any crash the cursor and the events agree
A stale worker with an old epoch cannot move the cursor
Lag per stream is available as now minus the watermark
not_expected: It does not poll or fetch
It does not decide when a cursor is too old; the app does (410)
It does not hold document content

algorithm.name: Transactional outbox with epoch fencing and watermark
algorithm.formula: commit iff epoch_in = epoch_stored ; watermark = min over partitions of last committed event time
steps: Open a transaction; check epoch_in equals the stored epoch
Insert the batch of events into the outbox and update the cursor and watermark in the same transaction
Commit; a relay publishes outbox rows to ch_bus and marks them sent
On takeover, increment the epoch so the old owner's later commits fail
Compute lag as now minus watermark and expose it

definitions: w_i: last committed event time of partition i
math.derivation: The stream is only as caught up as its slowest partition, so the watermark is the minimum. Anything older than W is fully applied.
math.worked_example: Partitions committed at 12:00:05, 12:00:09 and 12:00:03: W = 12:00:03. At 12:00:30, lag = 27 s. A freshness alert at 3 times a 60 s SLA fires at lag 180 s (t_t54).
math.complexity: O(1) per commit plus O(P) for the watermark minimum.
failure_modes: Relay crash between commit and publish: outbox rows stay unsent and the relay resumes, giving duplicates that ch_dedupe drops
Two workers with the same epoch from a bug: the compare-and-set on epoch allows one commit and rejects the other
math.calibration: Alert at 3 times the connector SLA (t_t54); review the multiple after a month of false alarms.

alternatives.name: Save the cursor in the poller's memory or a file
alternatives.why_rejected: A crash moves it out of step with the events.

alternatives.name: Write events and cursor to two stores
alternatives.why_rejected: No atomic commit across two stores.

security: Cursor theft or tampering: an attacker who edits a cursor could skip or replay; cursors are encrypted at rest and bound to (tenant, stream, epoch)
Zombie worker overwrite after a network partition: epoch fencing rejects it
Cross-tenant read of positions: row-level policy on tenant id plus tenant in the key
Cursor contents leak (some cursors embed ids): never written to logs, redacted in traces

performance.scaling: At 10x streams the table is small (about 200 bytes per stream); the outbox write rate is the limit and the table is partitioned by tenant.

edge_cases: Empty batch: cursor still advances, no outbox rows
Duplicate commit of the same batch: the compare-and-set on cursor makes it a no-op
Huge batch of 100,000 events: split into commits of 5,000 with the cursor updated only on the last
Concurrent pollers for one stream: fenced by epoch
Partial failure after outbox insert: transaction rolls back as a whole
Clock skew: watermark uses the source's event times, never the local clock for ordering
Reset after 410: cursor cleared, epoch bumped

ch_dlq.line:
Parked events with error class, retry history and one-click replay
replay <= 10% of rate budget; kept 30 days
ch_dlq.dumb: When a change cannot be handled after several tries, we do not throw it away or keep trying forever. We park it here with the reason it failed and a log of every try. A person can look, fix the cause, and replay it with one click. Replay is slowed down so it cannot swamp the app.
ch_dlq.inn: Events from ch_dedupe and ch_wf {event envelope, error_class, attempts, history[{at, error, ms}]}.
ch_dlq.out: Replay of a chosen event or batch to ch_wf; depth by error class to op_health.
ch_dlq.store: Rows {tenant, event envelope, error_class, attempts, history, parked_at, state} for 30 days (design). Envelopes carry ids only, with no document bodies.
ch_dlq.fail: If the park write fails the event stays on the bus and the consumer retries 3 times over 5 s, then pauses the partition rather than dropping it. A replay that fails again returns the event to the queue with the history extended; after 3 replays it is marked 'needs engineering'.
ch_dlq.hard: Error classes are a starting list (transient exhausted, poison, permission denied, not found, version regression); real traffic will add more.
ch_dlq.prop: Proposal: a lossless place for failures with a safe replay path keeps a sync pipeline from silently losing events.

deep.purpose: Keep every unprocessable event visible and replayable, so a failure is a queue item with a cause, not a silent loss.
expected: Every event that exhausts retries appears here with its history
A replay after the fix applies the event once
Depth by error class triggers an alert before it becomes a backlog
not_expected: It does not retry automatically; replay is deliberate
It does not store document bodies
It does not hide poison events; they are flagged to engineering

algorithm.name: Classified parking queue with throttled replay
algorithm.formula: replay_rate <= share * budget ; alert iff depth(class) > threshold
steps: Receive a failed event with class, attempts and history
Persist it and update the depth counters by class
Alert when depth exceeds the threshold or any poison event appears
On replay, check the class's cause is cleared, then resend to ch_wf under the replay rate cap
After success mark resolved; after 30 days expire

params.alert_depth: 0.5% of the last 24 h event count or 1 poison event (design; tune)

definitions: budget: requests per second for the app
share: fraction of budget replay may use
math.derivation: Replay is capped to a share of the app's budget so recovery never starves live sync.
math.worked_example: N = 12,000 events, budget 5 req/s, share 0.10: rate 0.5 per s, so 12,000 / 0.5 = 24,000 s, about 6.7 h. At 25% share the recovery takes 2.7 h.
math.complexity: O(1) per park and per replay; counters are O(classes).
failure_modes: Mass parking after an app outage: bulk replay by class with the throttle
Replay loop on an unfixable event: capped at 3 replays then flagged
math.calibration: Raise the replay share during off-peak hours only after live lag stays under SLA for 1 week.

alternatives.name: Infinite retry
alternatives.why_rejected: One poison event blocks a partition and burns the app's quota.

security: Sensitive data in a parked event: envelopes hold ids and error text only, and error text is scrubbed of tokens and urls with credentials
Operator replay abuse or replay of another tenant's event: replay needs an operator role, is tenant-scoped and audited
Poison event used as a denial of service: it parks after the retry bound and cannot block its partition
Replay used to roll back state: replay goes through ch_dedupe so old versions are dropped

performance.slo: park write p95 under 20 ms (design); replay starts within 1 min of the operator's click
performance.scaling: At 10x events the queue stays small if the DLQ rate stays under 0.5%; if not, the root cause is fixed rather than the queue sized.

edge_cases: Empty queue: nothing to show, alert disarmed
Duplicate park of the same event: keyed by (tenant, uri, version), second is merged into the history
Huge history of 1,000 tries: capped to the last 50 entries
Concurrent replay clicks: second is rejected while the first is running
Partial failure on replay: remaining events stay parked
Unicode in error text: stored as UTF-8 and escaped on display
Expiry while parked: operator warned 3 days before the 30-day limit

edges.d: Read {tenant, doc_id} to get stored version and deleted_at for the compare-and-set
Last applied source time {tenant, app, stream, applied_modified_at} for lag = now - applied
Progress {tenant, app, crawled, total_estimate, gaps[]} for the coverage estimate
Requests used {tenant, app, requests_per_s} so live polling keeps its share
Purge job {uri, tenant, stores[vectors, postings, snippets, acl]} after the soft delete
Floor {tenant, doc_id, floor_version} so older events cannot resurrect the document
Time and digest root {stream, last_sweep_at} so the sweep knows its age
Watermark {tenant, app, stream, watermark} per stream
Depth {tenant, app, error_class, count, oldest_age_s} by class
